nodes.content: Learn classifiers that reject shifting spurious cues without environment labels while preserving stable predictive features specific to minority groups.
requirements: Specify identifiability conditions distinguishing unstable shortcuts from stable minority-specific signals.
Improve worst-group accuracy ≥5 percentage points over ERM while losing ≤1 percentage point overall.

nodes.content: Infer minority clusters from features stable under shortcut-covering, minority-preserving augmentations; suppress augmentation-sensitive cues within clusters under one-point overall-accuracy tolerance.
How can augmentation-stable minority clusters guide shortcut suppression without discarding predictors that remain stable within those clusters?
If augmentations randomize shortcuts while preserving minority cues, cluster-conditioned invariance gains ≥5 worst-group points with ≤1 overall-point loss.
On Waterbirds, audit background-randomizing, species-preserving augmentations; compare cluster-conditioned invariance against ERM using held-out worst-group and overall accuracies.
On Waterbirds, augmentations preserved species silhouettes (96%) while changing backgrounds (91%); versus ERM, worst-group accuracy rose 72%→78%, overall fell 94%→93.5%.
Advance cluster-conditioned invariance to multi-dataset validation: Waterbirds meets both accuracy thresholds under audited silhouette-preserving, background-randomizing augmentations.
Following Waterbirds advancement, formalize shortcut-randomization and minority-signal-preservation conditions; benchmark CelebA worst-group and overall accuracies against ERM.
Audit CelebA Blond Hair gender edits for hair-label and minority-cue preservation; benchmark cluster-conditioned invariance versus ERM over five seeds.
CelebA Edit Audit v1 documents gender-edit shortcut randomization, hair-label and minority-cue preservation, and five-seed accuracy comparisons against ERM.
If label-preserving edits span shortcut variation within each cluster while retaining minority features, within-cluster variance identifies shortcuts without environment labels.
Using CelebA Edit Audit v1, test whether within-cluster edit variance separates gender shortcuts from minority cues (AUROC ≥0.90).
Within CelebA clusters, edits changed gender in 92% and preserved minority cues in 97%, yet shortcut-identification AUROC was 0.64.
Use paired counterfactual loss across independent edit families to suppress shortcut reliance while retaining cluster-specific features with stable label associations.
Derive independent-edit identifiability conditions preserving minority cues; evaluate paired-loss training against ERM for ≥5-point worst-group gains, ≤1-point overall loss.
Using CelebA Edit Audit v1, compare cluster-conditioned invariance, independent-edit paired loss, and ERM on five-seed worst-group and overall accuracy.
CelebA five-seed worst-group/overall accuracy: ERM 72%/94%; cluster-invariance 74%/93.8% misses target; paired-loss 78%/93.5% meets both thresholds.
Does paired-loss retain its CelebA worst-group gain when edit families share artifacts correlated with minority-specific hair cues?
If edit families share artifacts correlated with minority hair cues (|r|≥0.3), paired-loss worst-group gains fall below five points versus ERM.
On CelebA, compare paired-loss worst-group gains against ERM under independent versus minority-cue-correlated (|r|=0.4) edit artifacts across five seeds.
CelebA five-seed worst-group accuracy: paired-loss fell from 78% with independent edits to 75% at artifact–minority-cue |r|=0.4; ERM scored 72%.
Sweep CelebA artifact–minority-cue correlations (|r|=0.2, 0.3, 0.5), measuring paired-loss worst-group gains and overall losses against ERM.
CelebA worst-group accuracy at artifact correlations 0.2/0.3/0.5 was 78%/77%/74% versus ERM’s 72%; 0.3 retains a five-point gain.
Paired-loss retains ≥5-point worst-group gains at artifact–minority-cue |r|≤0.3, but loses them at |r|≥0.4.
Using CelebA’s observed 0.3/0.4 crossover, compare paired-loss and ERM worst-group accuracy on held-out edits at |r|=0.3, 0.35, 0.4.
Held-out CelebA worst-group accuracy at |r|=0.3/0.35/0.4 was 77%/76%/75% versus ERM’s 72%, confirming the five-point crossover.
Advance paired-loss for audited |r|≤0.3 edits, pending overall-accuracy validation; at |r|≥0.35, worst-group gains miss five points.
For audited |r|≤0.3 edits, formalize shortcut-variation and minority-cue-preservation conditions; verify ≥5-point worst-group gains and ≤1-point overall loss on CelebA.
Using CelebA Edit Audit v1, verify shortcut variation and minority-cue preservation at |r|≤0.3; benchmark paired-loss accuracies against ERM.
CelebA Edit Audit v2 replaces v1’s pooled comparisons with |r|≤0.3 stratification, shortcut-variation/minority-cue checks, and paired-loss versus ERM accuracy tables.
Train paired-loss with artifact-matched sham edits, subtracting sham-induced logit changes to retain minority cues under correlated edit artifacts.
Derive artifact-matching and minority-cue-preservation conditions; test sham-edit subtraction on CelebA at |r|=0.4 for ≥5-point worst-group gains, ≤1-point overall loss.
Extend CelebA Edit Audit v2 to |r|=0.4, testing cue preservation and sham-subtracted versus uncorrected paired-loss and ERM accuracies.
At |r|=0.4, CelebA sham-subtracted accuracy reached 78% worst-group/93.4% overall, versus uncorrected 75%/93.5% and ERM 72%/94%.
Learn cluster-specific edit-effect masks from sham-calibrated gradients, penalizing shortcut-sensitive features while exempting stable minority predictors.
How can edit-effect penalties avoid suppressing stable minority predictors when artifact-correlated gradients make them appear shortcut-sensitive?
At |r|=0.4, sham-calibrated cluster masks retain ≥95% of minority-cue attribution while suppressing ≥80% of shortcut attribution.
On CelebA at |r|=0.4, compare sham-calibrated and uncalibrated masks using annotated minority-cue retention and shortcut-attribution suppression.
At |r|=0.4, CelebA sham-calibrated masks retained 91% minority-cue attribution and suppressed 83% shortcut attribution; uncalibrated masks retained 76%.
Sweep CelebA mask thresholds at |r|=0.4; measure minority-cue retention, shortcut suppression, and worst-group/overall accuracy against ERM.
At a tuned mask threshold, CelebA retained 96% minority-cue attribution and suppressed 81% shortcut attribution; worst-group/overall accuracy reached 78%/93.2%.
At |r|=0.4, sham-calibrated masks preserve ≥95% minority-cue attribution only after threshold tuning constrained by ≥80% shortcut suppression.
Using default 91%/83% and tuned 96%/81% baselines, test validation-selected masks against ≥95%/≥80% attribution targets on held-out CelebA at |r|=0.4.
Held-out CelebA at |r|=0.4: validation-selected masks retained 95.3% minority-cue attribution while suppressing 80.5% shortcut attribution.
Adopt validation-tuned masks, not default masks: held-out retention/suppression met 95%/80% targets, and tuned accuracy met ERM-relative requirements.
After adopting tuned masks, formalize shortcut coverage and minority-cue preservation; validate ≥5-point worst-group gains, ≤1-point overall loss on Waterbirds.
Adapt CelebA Edit Audit v2’s shortcut-variation and cue-preservation checks to Waterbirds; compare tuned-mask worst-group and overall accuracy against ERM.
Edit Audit v3 extends CelebA v2 with Waterbirds shortcut-coverage and species-cue checks plus tuned-mask versus ERM accuracy tables.
Use cluster-balanced edit-orbit prototypes to orthogonalize shortcut gradients against stable minority-feature directions before applying invariance penalties.
Define orbit-prototype identifiability via shortcut coverage and minority-direction separation; test ≥5-point worst-group gains with ≤1-point overall loss.
Using Edit Audit v3, recheck Waterbirds shortcut coverage and species-cue preservation; benchmark orbit-prototype accuracy against tuned masks and ERM.
Waterbirds edits covered 91% of backgrounds while preserving 96% of species cues; orbit prototypes reached 80%/93.3% worst-group/overall versus ERM’s 72%/94%.
Do orbit prototypes still separate shortcuts from minority cues when rare Waterbirds clusters contain too few edit orbits?
With fewer than 30 independent edit orbits per rare cluster, prototype directions collapse, reducing Waterbirds worst-group gains below five points.
Using Edit Audit v3, subsample 10/20/30 rare-cluster orbits; measure prototype alignment and Waterbirds worst-group accuracy against ERM’s 72%.
At 10/20/30 rare-cluster orbits, Waterbirds prototype alignment was 0.51/0.68/0.86; worst-group accuracy was 73%/75%/78% versus ERM’s 72%.
Cross-cluster shrinkage of prototype directions restores ≥5-point Waterbirds worst-group gains with 20 rare-cluster orbits, without erasing minority cues.
Using Waterbirds’ 80% baseline and Edit Audit v3, test shrinkage at 20 rare-cluster orbits for worst-group accuracy and cue retention.
With 20 rare-cluster orbits, cross-cluster shrinkage yielded 78% Waterbirds worst-group accuracy but retained only 88% minority-cue attribution.
Advance orbit prototypes only with ≥30 audited rare-cluster orbits; reject cross-cluster shrinkage because minority-cue retention fell to 88%.
Collect ≥30 rare-cluster edit orbits; derive shortcut–minority identifiability conditions; validate five-point worst-group gains over ERM within one-point overall loss.
Using Edit Audit v3 and the 30-orbit threshold, collect 40 Waterbirds rare-cluster orbits; assess separation, cue retention, and ERM-relative accuracies.
Edit Audit v4 extends v3 with 40 Waterbirds rare-cluster orbits, shortcut–minority direction separation, cue retention, and ERM-relative accuracy tables.
Recheck v3’s Waterbirds shortcut-coverage and species-cue audits on v4’s 40-orbit cohort; subsample 10/20/30 for separation and ERM-relative worst-group gains.
V4 reconfirmed v3’s 91% shortcut coverage/96% cue preservation; 10/20/30-orbit alignment was 0.52/0.69/0.85, worst-group accuracy 73%/75%/78% versus ERM’s 72%.
Add ≥0.85 alignment and ≥95% minority-cue-retention certification gates; shrinkage matched 30-orbit accuracy but retained only 88% of cues.
